samples.text: There’s one very simple technique you can do at any time to feel a deeper connection to your inner child. Place one hand on the center of your chest (heart chakra), to feel a connection to love. Place the other hand on the center of your solar plexus just under your chest (solar plexus chakra) to feel a connection to your inner child. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One slap there hurts quite a lot, and so it’s natural to feel the vulnerable inner child living in this region. Now imagine sending love from the heart to the inner child, then receiving love from inner child and sending back to heart, in an infinite beautiful loop!

You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land.  And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it. Maybe what's actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you're in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

One awful conversation can leave you pretty certain you've finally figured somebody out. Then they come back later and actually deal with what you raised. They may still disagree with you, and you may still hate the boundary they're holding. One fight can be awful without being the whole pattern. [Lindsay Gibson's work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) on emotional immaturity looks at what keeps happening across different conversations.

They may still think your no is unfair after you've explained it as well as you know how. Maybe the first explanation really was bad, so you try again and the second one is clearer. That happens too. But sometimes they understood you already. They just want a different answer. You can keep rewriting your explanation forever if what you're waiting for is agreement.

When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to the kid for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you love in a super special way that makes you want to raise children together. Don’t imagine you love each other just because you want each other. Don't feel pressure to promise commitment; it comes by itself naturally & honestly as your hearts sync. Learn about each other before getting too close, and make sure to keep friends and community around who know both of you.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? But looking back on it now, I could have just seen it as some kind of mental illness rather than "lying" since there was no strategy behind it, and in fact she was usually quite honest.

You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and still be perfectly capable of thinking a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, use them; say the thing aloud, write it, whatever gets it out of the strange imaginary-conversation zone. And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it. Maybe what's actually happening is a knot in your stomach, an urge to leave, some image that keeps coming up, a song that suddenly feels relevant. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be kind.

If you really did hurt them, there is something to repair. An apology can get bigger than you meant it to. You meant to own one thing you did, and ten minutes later you're wondering whether you were allowed to have the complaint at all because they're still upset. Maybe you were wrong about more than you first thought; that happens. But if you're trying to work out how much of the argument was actually yours, feeling guilty is pretty poor evidence. Same with deciding they're manipulating you.

One awful conversation can leave you pretty certain you've finally figured somebody out. Then they come back later and actually deal with what you raised. They may still disagree with you, and you may still hate the boundary they're holding. I wouldn't know what to make of the first fight after that except that it was awful. What I'd watch is whether the same kind of ending starts showing up in completely different conversations. [Lindsay Gibson's work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) on emotional immaturity is helpful there. Different subject, same ending: somehow your experience is the part that never gets much room.

You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns you: you're supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Pema Chödrön calls this tightening and urge before the story has finished forming, "shenpa." Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.

Once my body softens a little, I don't have to use that opening to go looking for pain. I can bring to mind a pet, a baby, a friend, a partner, or anyone I naturally love. I feel the real love that's already there and see if some of it can move from my heart toward the younger part around the solar plexus, then back up again.

If you really did hurt them, repair it. You can own what you did and still notice yourself backing away from the complaint because their disappointment is hard to tolerate. Maybe you say it again because the first explanation really wasn't clear. But eventually you may notice you've already said what mattered and said no; what you're still waiting for is their understanding. It may not come. Guilt doesn't tell you how much of the conflict is yours, and it doesn't prove manipulation. The conversation can end with the misunderstanding still there.

It's hard to find sexually monogamous animals, have you ever looked? And as it turns out, we humans aren't a natural exception to the rule, either.  Plenty of tribal cultures were (and some still are) much looser about this, while still generally retaining the primary-partner "social monogamy."  Sexclusivity started gaining sway around the time we started planting carrots and peas, and owning land. That's when it made sense to keep track of how to keep our land in the family bloodline. By the Industrial Revolution, this ironically bureaucratic basis of romance became the only definition of marriage, by law.  I'm not trying to say we're just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans  tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity. And now we've gone one step further, so that even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That's why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on  when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can't fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let's see if I can fix that."

I took exclusivity further than that. B. wanted to marry me, but I was still attracted to other women, and somehow I decided that meant I shouldn’t marry her yet. I told her, “It’s not fair of me to commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let me see if I can fix that.”

It's not that I can't access the love, but the love seems unsafe. My inner child is sitting there observing its grown-up self and saying, “Yeah, that doesn't look like things went well for us.” Then I find myself getting resentful at the child and saying, “Well, you're the one who was the child and you have the opportunity to grow up.” I end up at war with the younger version who didn't do what they were supposed to do, while the older version is trying to make this vow of protection and nurturing. And the child is sitting there thinking, “Big fuckity whoopty doo. What are you gonna do for me?” Relaxation hasn't really affected that awkward, difficult time with the inner child for me.

One ugly conversation can feel like a revelation. Maybe it was. But if the same person comes back later and can actually stay with what you raised, while still disagreeing with you and keeping a boundary you hate, that matters too. One fight isn't a personality test. Then there is the pattern that keeps returning: you bring up something that hurt, and by the end you're carrying their reaction while your own experience has gone missing. That's closer to the territory [Lindsay Gibson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) describes in her work on emotional immaturity.

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none. I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.” I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.

Sexual exclusivity got much more important once agriculture, property and inheritance entered the picture. By the Industrial Revolution, the strict version was everywhere, with law and social pressure behind it. Plenty of tribal cultures have been much looser about what could happen outside a primary partnership, including other sexual or emotional relationships. There’s a term for some of that: social monogamy.
